title: Max Depth of Tree
description: Depth of a node = 1 + the deeper of its two children. Null subtree contributes 0.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"So I need to return the maximum depth of a binary tree — by depth you mean the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, right? (As opposed to number of edges, which would be one less.)"

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Empty tree — return 0?
• Node shape — is it `{ val, left, right }` with `null` for missing children?
• Can values be anything (negative, duplicates), or does that not matter here?
• Any constraint on tree size — do I need to worry about recursion stack overflow for very deep trees?
sections.why: The node-count vs. edge-count distinction is the easy thing to get wrong — LeetCode uses node count (a single-node tree has depth 1), but some textbooks use edge count (depth 0). Asking up front avoids an off-by-one that doesn't surface until the test cases run. The stack-overflow question hints that you know recursion has a ceiling and have an iterative BFS in your back pocket if needed.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious recursive solution — there's no slower naive.
sections.say: "There isn't really a 'brute force' separate from the optimal here — the natural solution is already O(n). I'd describe it as: every node's depth is 1 plus the deeper of its two children. Base case: null contributes 0. Recurse left, recurse right, return `1 + Math.max(left, right)`. The whole algorithm is three lines."
sections.why: Some problems don't have a slow-then-fast arc — saying so out loud is better than inventing a strawman. Interviewers worry about candidates who pad their answer to fit a template; calling out that the natural solution IS optimal demonstrates judgment about when an optimization step is or isn't needed.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to pure tree recursion?
sections.say: "The depth of a tree is defined recursively in terms of the depth of its subtrees — that's the textbook signature of structural recursion on a tree. Each node only needs information from its two children to compute its own answer, and those children compute the same way. So I'd reach for pure recursion: base case at null, combine the two children's answers, return. No need for BFS, no need for memoization, no need for an accumulator parameter. If interview constraints forbid recursion — say, the tree is a million levels deep — I'd switch to BFS with a queue and count levels, but for a typical interview tree, recursion is the cleanest expression."
sections.why: Naming the pattern *and* the property that makes the pattern apply is the move. 'Tree recursion' alone is a guess; 'tree recursion because depth is a recursive function of subtree depths' is the derivation. The unprompted callout to BFS as a stack-safe fallback is bonus: it shows you know the standard alternative without being asked.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the classic balanced tree, the empty tree, and a left-skewed tree that stresses the recursion depth.

examples.note: Classic balanced — the deeper path is root→20→either 15 or 7.
examples.trace:
maxDepth(3)
  maxDepth(9) → no children, 1 + max(0, 0) = 1
  maxDepth(20)
    maxDepth(15) → 1 + max(0, 0) = 1
    maxDepth(7)  → 1 + max(0, 0) = 1
    return 1 + max(1, 1) = 2
  return 1 + max(1, 2) = 3

examples.note: Degenerate — base case fires immediately, no recursion.
Skewed → recursion depth equals node count. Stresses the stack.
examples.trace:
maxDepth(1)
  maxDepth(2)
    maxDepth(3)
      maxDepth(4)
        return 1 + max(0, 0) = 1
      return 1 + max(1, 0) = 2
    return 1 + max(2, 0) = 3
  return 1 + max(3, 0) = 4

sections.why: The skewed-tree trace surfaces the stack-depth concern in concrete form — recursion depth is O(h), which on a degenerate tree equals n. The empty-tree case defends the `if (!root) return 0` base — without it the recursion would crash on `null.left`. Both bugs are easier to catch on the whiteboard than after the interviewer points to a failing test.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Null root → returns 0 via the base case. ✓
• Single node → 1 + max(0, 0) = 1. ✓
• Left-skewed (degenerate to linked list) → recursion depth equals n; for a million-node skewed tree the call stack would overflow. The fix is iterative BFS with a queue counting levels.
• Right-skewed → same as above, mirror image.
• Perfectly balanced → recursion depth is log₂(n), totally safe.
• All-same values → depth doesn't depend on values, only structure, so identical to the same shape with distinct values."
sections.why: The skewed-tree call-out is the senior signal. Most candidates write the three-line recursion and stop; flagging that recursion depth equals tree height — and that for adversarial inputs the height can equal n — shows you understand the difference between O(h) space (the right bound) and O(log n) space (the bound you'd get only on balanced inputs). Interviewers either nod or say 'assume the tree fits in the stack' — either response is good.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — every node is visited exactly once. The work per node is constant: one comparison, one max, one addition. No memoization needed because the recursion tree mirrors the actual tree, no overlap.

Space is O(h) for the recursion stack, where h is the tree height. For a balanced tree that's O(log n); for a skewed tree it's O(n). If the input could be adversarial — a deliberately skewed tree larger than the JS engine's stack frame budget — I'd convert to an iterative BFS: queue, level counter, `queue.length` snapshot per level. Same O(n) time, O(w) space where w is the max level width.

If you wanted to extend to 'find the node at maximum depth' or 'minimum depth', the recursive skeleton is identical — only the combine step changes. Min depth has the gotcha that a node with one null child shouldn't claim depth 1 from that side; you have to special-case it."
sections.why: The O(h) vs O(log n) distinction is the right defense against pushback. Calling out the iterative BFS fallback unprompted demonstrates you see the template, not just this solution. The min-depth extension is a real interview gotcha — LeetCode 111 — and naming it shows you've thought about the family of problems that share this shape, not just the specific question being asked.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the recursive max-depth on a real tree. The trace simulates the recursion with an explicit post-order stack so each call's depth is computed bottom-up. Pick an example and scrub.
trace: if (!arr || arr.length === 0 || arr[0] == null) return null;
const root = { val: arr[0], left: null, right: null };
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.left = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.left); }
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.right = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.right); }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter maxDepth — tree ${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { treeShape: input, root: root ? root.val : null } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'root is null → return 0', state: { treeShape: input, returns: 0 } };
yield { line: 3, label: `root=${root.val} not null — recurse`, state: { treeShape: input, root: root.val } };
yield { line: 5, label: `call maxDepth(${node.val}) — first visit, descend to children`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, stackDepth: stack.length } };

yield { line: 5, label: `return maxDepth(${node.val}) = 1 + max(${leftD}, ${rightD}) = ${d}`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, leftDepth: leftD, rightDepth: rightD, depthOfNode: d, stackDepth: stack.length } };
yield { line: 5, label: `root depth = ${ans}`, state: { treeShape: input, returns: ans } };

notes: Base case must return 0 for null — otherwise you would over-count by 1 at every leaf.
Use Math.max of the two recursive calls, then add 1 for the current node.
Space is O(h) where h is the tree height — O(n) worst case for a skewed tree, O(log n) for balanced.

alternates.label: Iterative BFS (level count)
alternates.when: Switch to this when the tree could be adversarially skewed and big enough to blow the recursion stack (~10k+ deep in V8). Also the right move if the interviewer asks for an explicit iterative solution or you're already standing up a queue for related level-order work.
notes: One outer iteration per level → depth = number of times the queue drains. No per-node depth bookkeeping needed.
Build the next level into a fresh array instead of shift()-ing the queue — shift() is O(n) on a JS array, so the array-swap pattern keeps the loop O(n) total.
Space is O(w) where w is the max level width. For a balanced tree that's O(n/2) at the bottom level — heavier than recursion's O(log n) average, but bounded by tree shape, not call-stack ceiling.

questions.q: Base case return value for a null node?
options: null
questions.explain: A missing child contributes zero depth; the +1 comes from the current node above it.

options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explain: Every node is visited exactly once.

options: O(h) where h is tree height
Always O(log n)
Distributing the +1 inside changes the precedence so the result is off by one
They produce different answers because Math.max short-circuits on the smaller branch
Both work, the first is cleaner
The inner form forces eager evaluation of both branches, doubling the recursion cost

questions.q: Max-depth is naturally a DFS (post-order) computation. Why post-order specifically?
options: Post-order is the only DFS order that visits each node exactly once on a binary tree
A node's depth needs BOTH children's depths computed first, then combines them — that bottom-up order IS post-order
Pre-order would over-count by 1 at every leaf because it adds before recursing
Post-order keeps the recursion-stack frames in left-then-right order, matching Math.max's argument evaluation
questions.explain: You can't compute `1 + max(left, right)` until you have the subtree results, so the work happens on the way back up — the defining trait of post-order DFS.

questions.q: You could also solve max-depth with BFS. How does the BFS version compute the answer?
options: It returns the queue's maximum size during traversal, which equals the deepest level's width
It counts how many levels the queue-based level-order loop processes
It tracks the last node enqueued and returns its index in the level-order array
It runs until the queue is empty and returns the total number of enqueue operations
questions.explain: BFS processes the tree level by level; the number of levels it drains equals the max depth.

questions.q: For a left-skewed tree of n nodes (a straight chain), the DFS recursion stack space is:
options: O(log n)
O(n) — the chain forces recursion depth equal to node count
questions.explain: Space is O(h); a skewed tree has h = n, so the worst-case stack depth is O(n), not O(log n).

questions.q: Why `Math.max` of the two subtrees rather than `Math.min`?
options: Math.min would return 0 whenever one child is null, collapsing the depth to 1 for every internal node
Depth is the length of the LONGEST root-to-leaf path, so we keep the deeper subtree
Math.min ignores null subtrees by default, which would skip whole branches of the tree
min is used for the related minDepth problem with no extra care needed
questions.explain: Maximum depth follows the longest path; min would compute a different (and trickier — null children must be excluded) quantity.

L3.prompt: Write `maxDepth(root)` returning the height of a binary tree. Log `maxDepth(root)` for the tree [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7].
